title: Mains electricity — AC, DC and your home's wiring
examTip: Favourite exam questions: wire colours, what each wire does, and how the earth wire keeps you safe. Learn them by heart.
introTips: Before reading, try to recall the colour and job of each wire in three-core cable. Check your answers as you go.
Before reading, think about why a live wire can be dangerous even when a switch is off.
intro: When you plug in a kettle, charge your phone or switch on a light, you use a carefully designed system. It keeps you safe from potential differences that could kill. The UK mains supply is an alternating potential difference of about 230 V. That is enough to kill. Yet people use it millions of times a day without harm. That safety comes from smart engineering. It uses the right wires in the right colours. Earth connections also drain dangerous current away from you.

keyPoints.heading: AC vs DC
keyPoints.content: Direct current (DC): a direct potential difference stays in one direction, so the current flows in one direction only. It comes from cells, batteries and solar panels. It is used in phones, laptops and torches. Alternating current (AC): an alternating potential difference keeps reversing direction, so the current keeps reversing too. The UK mains supply is AC at about 230 V and 50 Hz (50 complete cycles per second).
writeBullets: DC — a direct potential difference. Current in one direction only. Comes from batteries and cells
AC — an alternating potential difference keeps reversing, so the current reverses. Comes from the mains supply
UK mains: about 230 V, 50 Hz (50 cycles per second)

keyTerms.def: A potential difference that stays in one direction, so current flows one way only. Produced by batteries and cells.
A potential difference that keeps reversing direction, so current reverses too. The UK mains is about 230 V, 50 Hz.
The number of complete AC cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz). UK mains = 50 Hz.

keyPoints.memTip: AC = Alternates, DC = Direct (one direction). The mains 'alternates'. Think of it swinging like a pendulum, back and forth 50 times a second.

keyPoints.heading: Three-core cable
keyPoints.content: Most appliances are connected to the mains using three-core cable. The insulation covering each wire is colour coded for easy identification. Each wire has a specific job. The live wire (BROWN) carries the alternating potential difference from the mains supply. The potential difference between the live wire and earth (0 V) is about 230 V. This is the dangerous wire. It may be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open. This is because it is still connected to the supply. The neutral wire (BLUE) completes the circuit and returns current to the supply. It is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V). But you should never touch any live circuit. The earth wire (GREEN and YELLOW stripes) is a safety wire. It stops the appliance becoming live. It connects the metal casing of the appliance to earth (0 V). Normally, no current flows through the earth wire. If the live wire touches the metal casing, current flows to earth through the earth wire. Memory trick: BLue = Neutral, BRown = Live (BLaNk = Blue Neutral; BRiLliant = Brown Live).
writeBullets: Live wire — BROWN. Carries 230 V AC from the supply. The most dangerous wire
Live wire — can be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open
Neutral wire — BLUE. Returns current to the supply. About 0 V
Earth wire — GREEN and YELLOW. A safety wire connecting the metal casing to earth
Earth wire — stops the appliance becoming live if there is a fault

keyTerms.def: The brown wire in three-core cable; carries the 230 V AC supply potential difference and is the most dangerous wire.
The blue wire; completes the circuit and returns current to the supply at approximately 0 V.
The green and yellow striped wire; a safety wire that connects the metal casing to earth and stops the appliance becoming live.

keyPoints.memTip: BLue Neutral, BRown Live. Or picture a bruise. BLue = Neutral is the 'safer' one. BRown is the 'live danger' one.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Learn the job of each wire exactly. The earth wire is a safety wire. It stops the appliance becoming live.

keyPoints.heading: Earthing
keyPoints.content: Earthing means connecting an appliance's metal casing to earth (0 V). This is done through the earth wire (green and yellow). Normally, no current flows through the earth wire. The earth wire is a safety wire. It stops the appliance becoming live. Say there is a fault, and the live wire inside touches the metal casing. The earth wire gives a low-resistance path to earth. So most of the fault current flows through the earth wire, not through anyone touching the casing. A live wire may be dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open. It is still connected to the supply. Any connection between the live wire and earth is dangerous. Current can flow through that connection to earth. If the connection is a person, they get an electric shock. Electrical safety rules: - never use electrical appliances near water (water conducts electricity) - never overload sockets with adaptors - always check cables for damage before use
writeBullets: Earthing — connects the metal casing to earth through the green and yellow wire. Protects against electric shock
Earth wire — a safety wire that stops the appliance becoming live
Any connection between live and earth is dangerous. Current flows through it to earth
Safety rules: no appliances near water. No overloaded sockets. Check cables

keyTerms.def: Connecting the metal casing of an appliance to earth via the earth wire, so the appliance cannot become live.

keyPoints.memTip: Earth = escape route for fault current.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to think earthing prevents faults. It doesn't. It controls what happens when a fault occurs. The earth wire gives the fault current a safe route to earth.

0.question: What is the frequency of the UK mains AC supply, and what does this mean?
options: 50 Hz. There are 50 complete cycles every second
230 Hz. The potential difference is 230 V
50 Hz. The potential difference is 50 V
60 Hz. The same as the USA
0.correctFeedback: Perfect. 50 Hz means 50 complete cycles every second.
0.wrongFeedback: The UK mains is 50 Hz. Frequency means complete cycles per second. The 230 V is the potential difference, not the frequency.

1.question: What is the colour and potential difference of the live wire in three-core cable?
1.correctFeedback: Correct. The live wire is brown and carries the 230 V AC mains supply. It is the most dangerous wire in the plug.
1.wrongFeedback: The live wire is BROWN and carries 230 V AC. Blue is neutral (~0 V). Green and yellow is the earth wire, also ~0 V normally.

2.question: A switch in a mains circuit is open. Why can touching the live wire still be dangerous?
options: The live wire is still connected to the supply, so current can flow through you to earth
The neutral wire becomes live when the switch is open
The earth wire carries the full current when the switch is open
It is not dangerous, because no current can flow when a switch is open
2.correctFeedback: Correct. The potential difference between the live wire and earth is still about 230 V. If you touch it, current can flow through you to earth.
2.wrongFeedback: The switch does not disconnect the live wire from the supply. Any connection between the live wire and earth is dangerous. If that connection is you, current flows through you.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the live and neutral wire colours. Live is BROWN and neutral is BLUE. Many people swap these. Use BLue Neutral, BRown Live.
Thinking the earth wire carries current when working normally. It does not. Current only flows through the earth wire during a fault.
examTips: When explaining how earthing protects you, say that the earth wire stops the appliance becoming live. Fault current flows to earth through the earth wire, not through you.
